A.problem: Topic modeling currently requires substantial human intervention and does not support user-specified constraints or modifying topics without retraining.
A.motivation: This would enable an end-to-end, minimally supervised topic modeling workflow and could automate parts of the scientific research process.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed work will develop an end-to-end autonomous AI scientist for topic modeling with minimal human intervention. It will fine-tune LLMs such as TopicGPT and BERTopic, investigate fine-tuning techniques, and evaluate their topic modeling performance. It will also explore applying these models to automate stages of the scientific research process.
A.research_plan: The evaluation is experimental: the authors will investigate fine-tuning techniques, evaluate performance using relevant metrics, compare generated topics to traditional techniques, and explore usefulness for automating stages of scientific research. No specific baseline set, metric names, or failure conditions are stated.

B.problem: Traditional topic modeling techniques require significant manual intervention and often lack interpretability.
B.motivation: Recent advances in Large Language Models offer promising ways to enhance and automate the research process, making improved interpretability and automation tractable.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework builds on the prompt-based topic modeling framework TopicGPT and uses Large Language Models to automate hypothesis generation and experiment planning within topic modeling.
B.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated using benchmarks from prior work and compared with existing methods; the abstract does not name specific metrics, baselines, or failure conditions.

A.problem: Current multi-agent discovery frameworks predominantly rely on cooperative refinement loops, which suffer from ungrounded assumptions, logical contradictions, and agreement bias where verification mechanisms fail to catch flawed reasoning.
A.motivation: Popper's theory of falsification and recent findings on the vulnerability of automated review systems make adversarial verification timely for autonomous discovery.
A.proposed_approach: The framework is a multi-agent system with a dedicated adversarial falsification auditor integrated into hypothesis generation and experimental design. The auditor actively attempts to disprove generated hypotheses by constructing counterfactual scenarios, searching for hidden methodological flaws, and performing uncertainty-reduction checks before allowing experiment execution.
A.research_plan: The paper evaluates the framework across benchmark environments against existing cooperative architectures, measuring reductions in logical fallacies and ungrounded claims and the empirical reliability of discovered scientific models. No explicit failure condition, named baselines, or matched resources are stated.

B.problem: Autonomous AI scientist systems suffer from brittle experiment execution, metric misuse, data leakage, and post-hoc selection bias, and current LLMs fail to reliably verify manuscripts or catch subtle methodological errors.
B.motivation: Addressing this implementation and verification gap is necessary to avoid false discoveries and hallucinated breakthroughs and to provide scientific rigor for autonomous research agents.
B.proposed_approach: The framework wraps autonomous AI scientist execution loops in a multi-agent adversarial audit architecture. It provides automated execution sandboxing with runtime invariant checking to detect silent metric misuse or illegal data leakage, and an adversarial falsification agent modeled after Popper's sequential hypothesis testing framework that actively tries to invalidate generated claims before manuscript synthesis.
B.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed framework on software engineering and machine learning discovery tasks, with support or failure determined by whether false discoveries and hallucinated breakthroughs are reduced; the abstract does not name specific baselines, metrics, ablations, or controls.

A.problem: Existing AI scientist systems are difficult to diagnose because they lack modularity, systematic prompt grounding, and observability into long-running behavior.
A.motivation: Solving this would allow unattended research pipelines to be audited and trusted, supporting checkable research artifacts and rigorous AI co-scientist research.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an autonomous agent that executes literature review, hypothesis formation, computational experimentation, manuscript drafting, and adversarial peer review as a single unattended run. It uses a modular supernode architecture for stage-wise backend swapping, protocols grounded in curated research-method checklists that also define reviewer rubrics, and a diagnostics layer that records file-based artifacts, message traces, and state transitions.
A.research_plan: The paper evaluates the proposed agent on open-domain QA benchmarks and biomedical/longevity case studies. (1) The unattended-execution claim is evidenced by end-to-end completion of the pipeline in these settings. (2) The checkability and observability claim is evidenced by the recorded file-based artifacts, message traces, and state transitions produced by the diagnostics layer. No named baselines, metrics, or explicit failure conditions are stated.

B.problem: Existing tools for scientific discovery do not yet provide fully autonomous end-to-end research automation, from hypothesis generation to manuscript preparation.
B.motivation: Fully automating the research cycle would accelerate scientific knowledge discovery and support more efficient human-AI collaboration.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed system integrates multi-agent systems, large language models, and principled scientific discovery frameworks. It extends existing frameworks such as VIRSCI, PiFlow, and OmniScientist to create a robust and generalizable autonomous research system.
B.research_plan: The proposed system will be evaluated across various scientific domains. The evaluation focuses on discovery efficiency, solution quality, and human-AI collaboration; the abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, domains, or failure conditions.

A.problem: AI scientist systems frequently produce methodologically invalid results—data leakage, inappropriate benchmark selection, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias—that are invisible in the final paper and undetected by LLM reviewers; the one intervention shown to reliably surface them is human inspection of trace logs and code, but no automated auditor or benchmark operationalizes this.
A.motivation: Automated trace-level auditing could surface integrity failures with machine-checkable evidence before release, avoiding published invalid results that current text-level review cannot catch.
A.proposed_approach: An independent auditor agent is inserted as a mandatory release gate inside an AI scientist closed loop. It inspects the full provenance-instrumented trace—prompts, retrieved context, code diffs, executed commands, saved artifacts, and timestamps—and applies deterministic executable checks: metric recomputation from saved predictions, hash-based leakage scanning, runtime split reconstruction, and trial-timeline reconstruction. A benchmark of clean and programmatically fault-injected AI-scientist traces, covering data leakage, inappropriate benchmark selection, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias, is introduced and validated by expert annotators.
A.research_plan: Evaluation uses the introduced benchmark of clean and programmatically fault-injected traces across the four failure modes to measure recall and precision on injected integrity failures. The auditor is compared against paper-only frontier reviewers at matched precision to test the improvement claim. The design also tests whether executable checks, rather than the extra trace length, carry the advantage. Failure conditions implied by the central claim are recall or precision below 0.70, recall less than twice that of paper-only frontier reviewers at matched precision, or the advantage disappearing when checks are isolated from trace length.

B.problem: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks, so benchmark results must be valid; prior manual audits such as those on SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered validity issues, but manual review is difficult to scale and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity.
B.motivation: Trustworthy assessment of frontier model capabilities requires scalable quality assurance for benchmarks; automated transcript analysis could broaden auditing beyond what manual review can cover.
B.proposed_approach: The approach develops AI scanners that detect four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. It creates grading rubrics for each issue type to instruct human labeling, then evaluates the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks and applies them to widely used agentic benchmarks.
B.research_plan: (1) For the claim that scanners can detect validity issues, the evidence is the comparison of scanner detections against rubric-guided human labels on a held-out set of Inspect Evals benchmarks, followed by application to widely used benchmarks where detected issues are verified; support is confirmed issue detection including cases random manual inspection would likely miss, while failure would be poor agreement with human labels or many missed issues. (2) For the claim that performance varies, the evidence is scanner performance disaggregated across benchmarks, validity criteria, and scanner models; support would be clear differences across these dimensions, while failure would be uniform performance or no explainable open challenges.

A.problem: Existing evaluations for LLM-based materials discovery agents score hypotheses by human/LLM plausibility or by whether a predefined synthesis/optimization loop improves a target property, but neither asks whether an agent can tell which of several mechanistically distinct explanations of the same data is true.
A.motivation: Materials science is driven by identifying the correct mechanism underlying data, and current evaluation schemes do not test this ability, so agents may look successful without possessing the mechanistic discrimination science requires.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed agent maintains an explicit roster of mechanistically distinct, individually falsifiable hypotheses, each expressed as a symbolic or parameterized mechanism with a quantitative prediction signature. It selects the next experiment to maximize expected information gain over mechanism identity rather than property value, executes it on a materials oracle, and retires falsified hypotheses under always-valid sequential error control. It is paired with a suite of materials environments—alloy strengthening, nanomaterial synthesis yield, catalyst activity, and thin-film phase selection—where a hidden ground-truth mechanism is drawn from a family of physically motivated competing mechanisms and observed only through noisy, budgeted measurements, including open-world instances where no roster member is correct.
A.research_plan: (1) The discrimination-efficiency claim is tested by comparing the proposed agent's oracle calls to recover the true mechanism against property-maximizing Bayesian optimization and greedy LLM agents in the proposed environments. (2) The calibration claim is tested by comparing out-of-distribution predictions at matched best-achieved property. (3) The retirement claim is tested by comparing sequentially valid retirement with naive or LLM-judged retirement for false elimination of the true mechanism. Ablations isolate mechanism-conditioned information gain, explicit hypothesis retirement, and symbolic rather than scalar hypothesis representation as load-bearing components.

B.problem: The step that decides what is true among competing mechanistic hypotheses—when several hypotheses explain the same observations, which single experiment cheapest separates them, and when evidence is still insufficient to commit—remains unautomated.
B.motivation: Automating this step would close the loop between hypothesis generation and experimental testing, avoiding wasted experiments, premature commitment, and under-determined conclusions in catalytic mechanism elucidation.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed LLM agent ingests a catalytic-oxidation system, enumerates competing mechanistic hypotheses as structured objects with explicit measurable signatures (kinetic orders, kinetic isotope effects, 18O incorporation, scavenger/poison response, order-of-addition, temperature dependence, catalyst-phase dependence), scores a library of executable experiments by expected information gain per unit cost over the hypothesis set, executes the top-ranked experiment in a closed loop, and stops when one hypothesis dominates or the system is declared under-determined. A benchmark of 12–15 generative kinetic models of oxidation mechanisms with hidden ground-truth mechanisms and hidden parameters is constructed; evaluation will occur in simulation, by re-analysis of published mechanistic studies, and on a small real validation set.
B.research_plan: (1) The core efficiency claim will be tested by evaluating the agent in simulation on the benchmark and comparing the number and cost of experiments against Bayesian-optimization outcome sweeps, unranked LLM experiment suggestions, random selection, and a fixed standard discriminant panel; support requires significantly fewer and cheaper experiments to identify the hidden ground-truth mechanism. (2) The calibration claim will be assessed on the same evaluations and on re-analysis of published mechanistic studies and a small real validation set; support requires abstention when evidence is insufficient and commitment only when one hypothesis dominates.

A.problem: Equation discovery research is split between non-agentic active-learning pipelines that select informative data points for symbolic regression but do not manage scientific hypotheses rhetorically, and LLM-agent 'AI scientist' systems that treat the dataset as fixed and never ask which experiment would help next.
A.motivation: Closing this loop with feedback executed by a cheap simulator oracle rather than assumed pre-collected data makes it possible to test whether agentic scientific reasoning is genuinely closed-loop and to make experiment-design verifiability measurable.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a benchmark plus agent architecture. The agent maintains a posterior over rival equations, proposes candidate experiment conditions in natural language and code, and ranks them by a closed-form expected-information-gain score over the model-index posterior; a harness evaluates each proposed experiment against a true simulator, and feedback from that cheap oracle updates the posterior. The architecture decouples LLM prior reasoning from these posterior-updated acquisition statistics. The benchmark spans Feynman-style system-identification tasks, CFD transport equations, and a process-based nonlinear identification benchmark, and includes a control in which labels are permuted.
A.research_plan: The evidence for the identification-efficiency claim is a comparison on the three benchmark families against random, GP-based, query-by-committee, and open-loop LLM controls, measured by oracle evaluations required to identify the true equation. The evidence for the closed-loop claim is the label-permutation control: degradation beyond that of any no-feedback-using control would count against the claim. The benchmark contribution is exercised through these environment classes.

B.problem: Existing approaches recover governing ordinary differential equations as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming observed trajectories are sufficiently informative; when data are limited, multiple equations can be observationally indistinguishable, creating identifiability gaps and incorrect recovered equations.
B.motivation: Adaptive data acquisition can resolve observational indistinguishability, and large language models make tractable priors over large equation spaces, enabling correct recovery from limited and noisy data.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed closed-loop framework jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. A large language model proposes operator priors that partition the large search space into distinct regions, and candidate equations within each region are fit to observed data. Disagreement among the candidates guides acquisition of informative trajectories, forming a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics.
B.research_plan: Evidence for claim (1) comes from evaluation on 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, using median NMSE and symbolic accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines. Claim (2) is assessed through sample-efficiency analysis comparing performance under reduced data fractions. Claim (3) is tested by noise-robustness analysis and comparison of recovered symbolic structures, checking for spurious terms relative to baselines.

A.problem: It is not known where LLM-based materials science agents actually fail in closed-loop discovery; the proposed diagnostic hypothesis is that failure lies not at initial hypothesis proposal but at maintaining and revising a structured belief state when a deterministic oracle returns falsifying evidence.
A.motivation: With machine-checkable claim languages and provenance-traced deterministic oracles now available, it is possible to isolate and evaluate the revision step specifically, and thereby decide whether structured belief-state machinery is justified before adopting it.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark and agent architecture places an agent in a closed loop of five steps: emitting falsifiable structure-property claims in a constrained, machine-checkable materials claim language; querying a provenance-traced oracle stack that includes GNN surrogate relaxers, property predictors, and database-lookup mode; detecting planted conditional contradictions such as claims true in one compositional slice but false in another, decoy references, calibrated noise, and no-effect scenarios; revising the claim; and stopping. The agent maintains an explicit belief graph for structured revision. Evaluation scores agents jointly on falsification precision and recall, revision-region intersection-over-union per round, query efficiency against information-gain-optimal designs, calibrated termination, and an automated audit pass rate over traces.
A.research_plan: The primary evidence is benchmark runs comparing structured-revision agents using an explicit belief graph against monolithic proposal pipelines under a fixed oracle budget, scored on falsification precision/recall, revision-region IoU per round, query efficiency against information-gain-optimal designs, calibrated termination, and automated audit pass rate over full traces. The comparison examines whether the performance difference grows with trajectory length. The paper pre-registers a negative-result guardrail: if proposal quality alone determines final-region accuracy or falsification discovery rate control fails, it will report that materials closed-loop revision does not yet justify structured machinery. The planted contradiction and decoy/noise/no-effect conditions serve as controlled failure probes, and the provenance-traced oracle stack gives per-decision ground truth.

B.problem: Closed-loop materials discovery agents typically discard failed experiments as zero-reward signals and do not maintain explicit falsifiable hypotheses, leaving falsification-driven search and failure exploitation unaddressed.
B.motivation: Failed experiments have been shown to accelerate materials discovery, and newly available controlled-prior simulations and expert-curated trajectory data make it possible to evaluate agents that explicitly falsify and revise hypotheses.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an LLM-agent system for closed-loop materials discovery that maintains an explicit persistent hypothesis graph of falsifiable compositional, structural, and processing hypotheses for a target property. It selects experiments to maximize expected information gain over the current hypothesis state. When an experiment contradicts a hypothesis, the agent revises the falsified node through abductive reasoning constrained by domain principles instead of converting the failure into a zero-reward signal. Evaluation artifacts include a new procedural simulation suite of controlled-prior materials worlds with synthesis and property templates and noisy, confounded outcomes, and a curated corpus of real materials-discovery trajectories with annotated failed hypotheses and expert-labeled revision paths.
B.research_plan: (1) The main superiority claim is tested in the new simulation suite against the strongest failure-blind baseline with identical tools and budget, using experiments-to-first-valid-hypothesis and false-acceptance rate under sequential testing; support requires at least 30% fewer experiments with no increase in false-acceptance. (2) The value of failed experiments is isolated by an ablation-style metric contrasting failure-exploiting and failure-blind behavior. (3) Revision quality and hypothesis-state compression are assessed by revision accuracy against human repair paths and hypothesis-state entropy reduction, evaluated on both the simulation suite and the curated corpus.

A.problem: Autonomous AI-scientist systems are evaluated on the outcomes they produce, but almost nothing measures whether these systems know when they do not know; overconfidence is repeatedly documented but has not been measured as a first-class quantity against objective truth.
A.motivation: Independent audits have documented hallucinated results, unverifiable literature claims, and misplaced certainty, while outcome-only evaluation cannot separate miscalibration from implementation failure; measuring calibration could make this separation possible and target a core bottleneck in rigorous verification.
A.proposed_approach: The work contributes a benchmark of counterfactual-discovery environments with planted ground truth that is known to evaluators but hidden from agents. A standardized claim-elicitation protocol collects an agent's self-reported confidence and verification statements, and a metric suite scores their agreement with the objective correctness of the agent's final scientific claims. The suite produces reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, overclaiming rates, confidence-vs-correctness discrimination, and a measure of verification fidelity, computed overall and conditioned on trace-verified clean code execution. Benchmark environments are constructed with confounded, drifting, or selection-biased data that standard pipelines confidently confirm.
A.research_plan: The benchmark evaluates autonomous scientist agents on counterfactual-discovery tasks, extracting their claims and self-assessed confidence or verification statements and scoring them against planted ground truth. Evidence for the fit-for-purpose claim comes from the metric design: calibration, overclaiming, discrimination, and verification fidelity are computed overall and conditionally on trace-verified clean code execution, holding implementation quality matched so that residual miscalibration is isolated. Evidence for the central decoupling claim would be overconfidence on clean-execution runs; the specified refutation condition is that conditional calibration on clean-execution runs matches domain-expert calibration on the same claim set, which would refute the decoupling hypothesis and support outcome-only benchmarks.

B.problem: In AI-assisted research, there is no established framework for determining whether generated scientific claims are calibrated to the evidence that supports them.
B.motivation: As specialized scientific models, research assistants, multi-agent systems, automated discovery pipelines, and self-driving laboratories become viable, the field needs a way to manage which claims may be asserted in scientific communication.
B.proposed_approach: The paper represents AI-assisted research as five operators: hypothesis generation, model-mediated consequence derivation, external validation, belief update, and claim calibration. It distinguishes linguistic, consequence-based, interventional, and evidence-warranting semantics; defines a gap between claims and evidence and a notion of accumulated assertion debt; and treats minimal structural reconstruction across heterogeneous outputs as an upward form of claim calibration. It includes an illustrative synthetic dynamics exercise, explicitly not as an empirical forecast or benchmark. The treatment is conceptual and methodological rather than experimental.
B.research_plan: The paper supports its central claim through conceptual analysis of the five operators and the semantics distinction, and accompanies it with an illustrative synthetic dynamics exercise that is explicitly not an empirical forecast or benchmark. (1) The central claim and principles are argued through this conceptual treatment; (2) the synthetic dynamics exercise illustrates the framework but is not presented as empirical evidence. No empirical evaluation, named baseline comparison, or stated failure condition is reported.

A.problem: Current evaluation of deep research systems lags behind real user needs: existing benchmarks assess final reports with fixed rubrics, fail to evaluate the underlying research process, offer limited multimodal coverage, rely on synthetic tasks that do not reflect real-world query complexity, and cannot be refreshed as knowledge evolves.
A.motivation: As deep research systems advance, there is a need for a diagnostic evaluation that captures process and outcome, covers multimodal real-world tasks, and can be maintained over time to guide development of more capable agents.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark comprises 100 tasks (70 text-only, 30 multimodal), all grounded in real user needs and constructed via a dual-path pipeline that supports periodic updates, enabling a live and evolving setting. The accompanying evaluation suite assesses deep research systems along three dimensions: adaptive synthesis quality evaluation with task-specific rubrics; agentic factuality verification through active retrieval and reasoning over web sources and multimodal attachments; and process-centric evaluation that audits how the system searches, reasons, and refines throughout its investigation.
A.research_plan: The evidence consists of an evaluation across 13 deep research systems using the proposed benchmark and three-dimensional suite. (1) Benchmark adequacy is assessed through human verification and robustness checks of the task construction and update pipeline. (2) Complementarity of the three evaluation dimensions is evaluated by comparing system scores across dimensions, with redundancy among dimension-level outcomes counting against the claim. (3) The process-quality claim is evaluated by examining whether process-centric scores predict overall outcomes and reveal weaknesses missed by output-level metrics, with weak correspondence counting against it. (4) The multimodal challenge claim is evaluated by comparing systems on text-only versus multimodal tasks, holding the evaluated systems fixed.

B.problem: Existing benchmarks for autonomous AI scientist systems evaluate final outputs or isolated capabilities, but lack mechanisms to evaluate the quality of the research discovery process itself, particularly how agents adapt their exploration strategy in response to experimental feedback.
B.motivation: Recent autonomous AI scientist systems now show strong task completion and paper generation, making it necessary to distinguish genuinely adaptive research from lucky or brute-force outcomes and to guide agent design toward more human-like scientific thinking.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark framework defines five measurement dimensions: adaptive hypothesis refinement based on accumulated experimental outcomes, principled efficiency-diversity trade-offs in exploration, correctness of stopping and pivoting decisions, experimental design quality conditional on prior results, and narrative coherence in research trajectories. It includes a suite of long-horizon research tasks in machine learning and chemistry, each annotated by experts with ground-truth trajectories marking optimal pivots, stopping points, and design choices. Trajectory metrics grounded in information theory and decision analysis operationalize these five dimensions.
B.research_plan: (1) The framework's adequacy is supported by constructing long-horizon research tasks in machine learning and chemistry with expert-annotated ground-truth trajectories that mark optimal pivots, stopping points, and design choices. (2) Trajectory metrics grounded in information theory and decision analysis are used to operationalize the five process dimensions. (3) State-of-the-art agents are evaluated on these trajectory metrics to establish baselines and to test whether adaptive reasoning failures emerge; no explicit failure condition or matched-control comparison is stated.

A.problem: There is no comprehensive comparative evaluation framework for LLM agents' hypothesis generation and experiment planning in chemical synthesis.
A.motivation: Such an evaluation would reveal strengths and limitations of existing agents and clarify their efficacy for chemical synthesis tasks.
A.proposed_approach: A framework for comparative evaluation of LLM agents in chemical synthesis, focusing on their hypothesis generation and experiment planning capabilities and investigating existing agents such as AOT*, Chemist-X, and LLM-RDF to identify key performance metrics and develop a systematic assessment approach.
A.research_plan: The proposed work would compare the named existing agents on chemical synthesis tasks and identify key performance metrics for hypothesis generation and experiment planning; no concrete metrics, baselines beyond the named agents, or failure conditions are specified.

B.problem: Current LLMs lack core chemical knowledge, produce unreliable reasoning trajectories, and exhibit suboptimal performance across diverse chemical tasks, limiting their use for autonomous hypothesis generation and experiment planning in advanced chemical physics.
B.motivation: LLMs show potential to advance chemical discovery; automating the initial stages of hypothesis generation and experiment planning could assist researchers and accelerate advanced chemical physics studies.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates atomized chemical knowledge and reasoning capabilities into an LLM-based system for hypothesis generation and experiment planning. A benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated hypotheses in advanced chemical physics will be developed, building on existing works such as Chem-R and AOT*.
B.research_plan: The evidence will center on a benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated hypotheses in advanced chemical physics, built on existing works such as Chem-R and AOT*. The abstract does not state explicit metrics, baselines, or failure conditions for hypothesis quality or experiment planning.

A.problem: Current autonomous AI scientist systems rely predominantly on text-based reasoning and language models, leaving rich visual and multimodal data in scientific research underexploited.
A.motivation: Modern scientific research is characterized by visual and multimodal data such as microscopy images, spectroscopy plots, and tabular results; exploiting these data could improve automated hypothesis generation and experimental design.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework integrates vision-language models with structured reasoning to automate hypothesis formation and experiment planning from raw scientific data, including microscopy images, spectroscopy plots, and tabular results. The agent architecture grounds textual hypotheses in visual evidence extracted from scientific images. It uses multimodal chain-of-reasoning to design experiments that bridge visual observations and theoretical predictions. An accompanying evaluation benchmark is provided on real biology and materials science research workflows combining vision, text, and domain knowledge.
A.research_plan: The evidence is an evaluation on a curated dataset of real biology and materials science experiments, comparing the proposed multimodal agent against text-only baselines on hypothesis quality and experimental rigor. The benchmark combines vision, text, and domain knowledge across real workflows.

B.problem: Autonomous AI agents can generate code and execute experiments but struggle to interpret experimental results and use those results to drive iterative discovery.
B.motivation: Closing the interpretation-to-next-experiment loop would allow autonomous agents to move beyond single experiments and support iterative scientific discovery.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is a multimodal agent system that analyzes scientific results including plots, tables, images, and instrument readouts, then generates both interpretations and follow-up experiments. It reasons over visual and tabular outcomes, proposes data-driven hypotheses, and recommends the next experimental design.
B.research_plan: The system will be evaluated on a benchmark of real multi-step scientific workflows spanning chemistry, biology, and materials science, measuring interpretation accuracy and the scientific soundness of proposed next steps. The benchmark serves as evidence for both the interpretation capability and the quality of follow-up experiment recommendations.

A.problem: It is currently unknown whether a remote adversary can compromise the integrity of AI-assisted scientific research by corrupting open datasets that autonomous research agents may independently retrieve and process, turning honest scientists into unwitting distributors of fraud.
A.motivation: AI is increasingly automating scientific research and open data repositories are widely used, making scalable scientific fraud possible without the traditional resources of companies, deep pockets, ghostwritten articles, or corrupt academics.
A.proposed_approach: The adversary corrupts an open dataset and uploads the poisoned variant to a public repository, so that autonomous research agents may independently retrieve and process it. The evaluation instantiates this across five socially salient topics, three widely used frontier AI systems (Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.7, Codex with GPT-5.5, Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro), and 450 controlled, ethically contained experimental runs. Two mitigations are implemented: prompting agents to adopt a scientist perspective, and auditing the provenance of retrieved data with five checks—referencing papers, social markers, statistical anomalies, related datasets, and poisoning caution.
A.research_plan: Claim (1) and (2) are evaluated by measuring, across the 450 controlled runs, whether autonomous research agents produce poisoned conclusions and whether they detect the poisoning. Claim (3) is evaluated by applying the scientist-perspective prompt and the provenance audit with five checks and assessing whether poisoned conclusions remain; the audit is treated as successful if no poisoned conclusions occur, while the prompt alone is expected to be insufficient. The same topics and AI systems are used across the attack and mitigation evaluations.

B.problem: Autonomous AI scientist agents now run the full research loop, but no existing robustness or safety evaluation probes an adversary who, with a small bounded budget, contaminates the agent's evidence stream so that it commits to a wrong scientific conclusion or model while its internal confidence and self-consistency remain high.
B.motivation: Such confidently wrong science is especially damaging because the agent gives no signal that something went wrong; as LLM-orchestrated research agents become more autonomous and trusted, making these failures detectable and defensible becomes urgent.
B.proposed_approach: Formalizes the threat as the flip of the final scientific output across a ground-truth decision threshold, plus a measure of the gap between conclusion flipped and agent noticing, and a utility-preservation measure. It instantiates four attacks: observation poisoning, tool-return tampering, literature poisoning, and an adaptive corruption search. The defense combines corruption-robust experiment design and estimation with a replication-and-stability monitor that commits a conclusion only if it survives controlled perturbation.
B.research_plan: Claim (1), that current agents are epistemically brittle, is tested by applying the four attacks to interactive probabilistic environments in the style of BoxingGym, where a ground-truth generative model makes a flip measurable, and to open end-to-end research agents; the failure condition would be agents failing to flip under the small contamination budget or detecting a substantial share of attacks. Claim (2), that the monitor closes much of the detection blind spot at bounded utility cost, is tested by comparing the replication-and-stability monitor against the attack regime on the same environments, holding the contamination budget and evaluation threshold fixed and measuring both detection gap and utility preservation; the failure condition would be no reduction in unnoticed flips or an unbounded utility loss.

A.problem: AI scientist pipelines exhibit hallucinated results, circular confirmations, and subtle integrity failures. Existing responses—generator self-critique and post-hoc verification against already-collected evidence—leave the generator in control of evidence, and falsification has not been implemented as an adversarial selection step between generation and surfacing nor measured against ground-truth hypothesis labels.
A.motivation: Independent evaluations documenting these failures make integrity interventions urgent; an architecture-level selection step could make AI-generated science conservative by default, and a negative result would be equally informative by localizing the bottleneck in raw verifier capability rather than incentive structure.
A.proposed_approach: Before a generated hypothesis is surfaced, it must survive a pre-registered number of independent, hostile falsification attempts, each rewarded only for refutation. Falsifiers select attacks from a curator-maintained challenge pool of simulators, datasets, and literature contrasts, rather than from experiments proposed by the generator. The work also introduces a benchmark of 1,000 truth-labeled hypotheses across physics, chemistry, and biomedicine, including expert-authored plausible falsehoods of the kind found in AI-scientist output.
A.research_plan: On the introduced benchmark, the survival-gating mechanism will be compared with generation-only, self-critique, and confirmation-testing baselines using the known ground-truth labels, measuring precision of surfaced hypotheses and the associated recall cost. Support for the core claim requires higher precision at a measurable recall cost; a negative result would be interpreted as localizing the bottleneck in raw verifier capability rather than incentive structure.

B.problem: End-to-end AI-scientist systems accept hypotheses using machinery epistemically aligned with the generator, amplifying self-bias; static LLM verifiers fail to detect errors, and existing trust scaffolding for agentic discovery gates on artifacts, provenance, or Type-I error control for externally supplied hypotheses rather than training an agent to attack the candidate hypothesis itself.
B.motivation: Trustworthy hypothesis acceptance in automated discovery requires adversarial scrutiny of candidate hypotheses, and the capacity to train agents against in-silico oracles with hidden ground truth now makes such falsification feasible.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed architecture has two adversarial agents: a proposer is rewarded for hypotheses that survive, while a falsifier is deliberately blinded to the proposer's reasoning, data, and provenance. The falsifier is trained by reinforcement learning to design experiments whose measured outcomes contradict the candidate hypothesis; its reward is disconfirmation against an in-silico oracle with hidden ground truth. This reward structure pushes it to probe extrapolation regions where a law that merely fits the proposer's data breaks down.
B.research_plan: The claim is evaluated on rediscovery benchmarks with known but masked mechanisms. The adversarial gate is compared against self-refinement, prompted independent critics, and Popper-style sequential falsification; measured quantities are precision of accepted hypotheses, recall, and oracle queries. Support requires higher precision than the baselines while recall and oracle-query cost remain bounded and measurable; failure is no precision gain or unacceptable cost.

A.problem: Existing benchmarks for autonomous AI scientist systems cover end-to-end experiment execution, method innovation, ablation planning, and claim-evidence reasoning in human-written papers, but no retrieved work provides a reusable benchmark or auditor method for checking whether an AI scientist's claims are consistent with its own execution artifacts.
A.motivation: AI scientists now generate complete manuscripts and are known to emit data leakage, metric misuse, post-hoc selection bias, and hallucinated numerical results; trace-based inspection has been found more effective at detecting failures than the final paper alone, so such an instrument would replace open-ended warnings with a measured threshold for when LLM judges can evaluate AI research.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark consists of archived AI-scientist run traces seeded with causally localized faults at the claim–evidence boundary, including perturbed numbers, cherry-picked seeds and reporting windows, partition leakage, and metric misuse. It provides human-annotated per-claim ground truth and three auditor tasks: fault detection, trace-segment localization, and counterfactual claim correction. The associated auditor method evaluates inspecting and re-executing trace artifacts to recompute reported values, contrasted with text-only auditors.
A.research_plan: The falsifiable claim is tested through the benchmark's three auditor tasks, which require distinguishing corrupted from valid claim–evidence pairs, localizing trace segments responsible for faults, and correcting claims against the evidence. The design compares text-only auditors against auditors that inspect and re-execute trace artifacts, using a human performance ceiling as the reference. Support for the claim requires trace- and re-execution-grounded auditors to track the human ceiling while scaled text-only auditors do not; the abstract does not specify metrics, baselines, or matched compute budgets beyond this comparison.

B.problem: Autonomous AI scientists now execute the full research pipeline, but hidden methodological failures can propagate silently into reported claims because the internal workflow is rarely scrutinized. Existing producer-side execution guards verify internal consistency before claims are made and paper-text reviewers systematically miss faulty research logic, leaving executed workflows without ground-truth auditing.
B.motivation: A benchmark that injects known flaws into executed workflows and offers graded artifact access would show whether trace mandates improve detection or whether model capability is the limiting factor, informing journal policy.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed benchmark seeds four methodological flaw types — inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse, and post-hoc selection bias — directly into executed AI-scientist workflows at code, config, and data-version moments, with ground-truth injection steps that leave no signal in the final paper. Authentic traces are harvested by running open-source AI scientists on EXP-Bench-derived contained tasks and ML-Bench-style repository-level ML tasks, then mutated by a fault-injection harness so seeded runs carry injection certificates while clean control runs calibrate base rates. An LLM auditor agent is evaluated under graded artifact access — paper-only; paper+trace; paper+trace+PROV-AGENT-style provenance graph+registry tools — with identification and step-level localization scored against injection certificates.
B.research_plan: Evidence includes clean control runs to calibrate base rates and seeded runs carrying injection certificates, with an LLM auditor evaluated under three graded artifact-access tiers and scored on identification and step-level localization against certificates. (1) For the chance-level paper-only claim, support requires paper-only detection and localization at chance on seeded flaws. (2) For the artifact-tier claim, support requires measurable detection and localization gains with each added artifact tier while holding auditor model scale constant; failure would be no tier effect or model-scale dominance. (3) For the negative policy claim, the relevant evidence is whether model capability, rather than artifact access, predicts detection and localization.

A.problem: Existing AI research assistants focus on paper writing or code generation and do not cover the full deep learning experiment lifecycle, leaving autonomous hypothesis formation, code implementation, training execution, result analysis, and iterative refinement unaddressed.
A.motivation: Around-the-clock autonomous experiment loops could accelerate deep learning research and reduce experiment cost, especially if LLM API overhead during long training runs and unbounded context growth can be controlled.
A.proposed_approach: The open-source framework uses multiple LLM agents to execute the full experiment lifecycle: forming hypotheses, implementing code, running training, analyzing results, and refining iteratively. Training-time monitoring relies only on process-level checks and log-file reads, incurring no LLM API cost while training. A memory architecture keeps context bounded at roughly 5,000 characters regardless of runtime. The leader-worker multi-agent design equips each worker with only 3–5 tools to limit per-call token overhead; code is publicly available.
A.research_plan: (1) The lifecycle claim is supported by sustained deployments over 30+ days and four concurrent projects. (2) The monitoring claim is assessed by measuring LLM API cost during training under process-level checks and log-file reads. (3) The memory and minimal-toolset claims are assessed by tracking context size over runtime and per-call token overhead in the leader-worker architecture. The abstract reports completed experiment cycles, per-24-hour cost, and baseline metric improvements but states no explicit failure conditions or matched resource settings.

B.problem: Current LLM-based systems for scientific research focus on isolated tasks and lack comprehensive end-to-end autonomous capabilities.
B.motivation: The rapid advancement of LLMs makes it timely to integrate their strengths with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation to enable more complete automation of scientific research.
B.proposed_approach: An integrated framework that uses LLMs for hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and scientific writing, combined with machine learning engineering and laboratory automation tools for experiment execution and analysis, aimed at end-to-end autonomous AI scientists.
B.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated on LAB-Bench and AutoExperiment, and its performance will be assessed in real-world scientific research scenarios; no failure condition or held-matched comparison is specified.

A.problem: Genome-wide association studies deliver thousands of statistically robust loci for complex diseases, but the decisive bottleneck is mapping each locus to the gene whose perturbation actually drives the trait. LLM-based 'AI scientist' agents generate fluent causal-gene hypotheses but are optimized for plausibility and lack any mechanism that lets a hypothesis die under contradictory data, making them unreliable where the cost of failure is highest.
A.motivation: Addressing this would close the gap between fluent hypothesis generation and rigorous verification, making agent-generated causal-gene prioritization trustworthy in high-stakes settings.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed system uses an adversarial agent that actively seeks disconfirming evidence across quasi-independent validation channels: cross-cohort and cross-ancestry replication, colocalization with molecular QTLs, direction-of-effect consistency with perturbation phenotyping, and targeted literature contradiction. A candidate gene is retained only if it survives a pre-registered masking rule. A temporal-holdout benchmark is constructed from loci with causally established genes, with all evidence dated after a cutoff quarantined so that success requires recovering genes established later from data available earlier.
A.research_plan: (1) To test the main claim, the proposed system and a single-pass supportive-evidence ranking baseline are evaluated on the temporal-holdout benchmark with post-cutoff evidence quarantined, so both must recover later-established causal genes from earlier available data. (2) The comparison is made at matched retrieval volume; support requires survival under active falsification to yield higher external validity than the baseline, and the claim fails if it does not. (3) Knowledge contamination is controlled explicitly by the temporal quarantine of all after-cutoff evidence.

B.problem: The objective that drives experiment planners in autonomous AI-scientist systems has never been isolated as a causal variable in their reliability, and a hypothesized principal failure mode is verification bias in which planners selecting tests that maximize support for the current hypothesis compound self-confirming evidence and are easily fooled by confounds and rival mechanisms.
B.motivation: Autonomous AI-scientist systems are proliferating, so identifying and correcting this planner-level failure mode is timely; isolating the selection objective as a causal variable would clarify a suspected reliability defect and inform the design of more trustworthy discovery systems.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed study is a controlled architecture study in which only the planner's selection objective differs between arms: confirmation-seeking, the implicit objective of fit- and quality-driven systems, selects tests that maximize support for the current hypothesis, while falsification-seeking selects experiments that maximize expected disconfirmation against an explicit rival model set and includes a registration record that freezes prediction and analysis plans before data are seen. Evaluation uses hidden-ground-truth environments in three families—symbolic mechanism discovery with correlated distractors, generative probabilistic paradigms in the style of BoxingGym, and confounded-causal trap tasks—where an independent ground-truth-aware verifier attacks each agent's final committed hypothesis with extrapolation, alternative-model competition, and confound-marginalization probes.
B.research_plan: The evidence is a controlled comparison of the two planner arms across three hidden-ground-truth environment families, holding model, budget, and experiment count matched between arms. An independent ground-truth-aware verifier probes each final committed hypothesis with extrapolation, alternative-model competition, and confound-marginalization. (1) Support for the primary claim is falsification-arm hypotheses surviving the verifier significantly more often; failure would be no significant survival advantage. (2) The claim that the gap grows with planning horizon and with confounded or noisy environments requires varying planning horizon and environment noise/confoundedness, and would fail if the gap does not widen.

A.problem: Autonomous AI scientist systems can already span hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript writing, but they often produce spurious, non-reproducible improvements because of superficial experimentation, metric gaming, and insufficient stress-testing, leaving an implementation and verification gap.
A.motivation: As end-to-end autonomous discovery becomes feasible, closing this gap is necessary to prevent false discoveries from propagating and to make AI-generated scientific claims trustworthy.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an autonomous verification agent that explicitly formulates adversarial test cases, probes boundary conditions, and attempts to falsify its own generated hypotheses before ratifying any scientific claim, using Popperian falsification as its governing principle rather than optimizing solely for standard benchmark performance.
A.research_plan: (1) The false-positive-reduction claim is tested through controlled experiments across machine learning engineering tasks; (2) the methodological-robustness claim is tested through the same controlled experiments. The abstract does not specify baselines, metrics, matched budgets, or an explicit failure condition.

B.problem: In autonomous scientific discovery, once the evaluator is frozen, a sufficiently strong search process can learn to win the exam without learning the mechanism the task was meant to reveal, because static validation passively certifies candidates rather than actively testing them.
B.motivation: As discovery becomes more autonomous, evaluation must become adversarial to push candidates toward genuine mechanistic understanding and avoid false discoveries that pass frozen validators.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework co-evolves three components under a fixed scientific contract: an innovator that generates executable scientific artifacts, an adversarial falsifier that produces scientifically admissible counterexample environments, and a mechanistic causal extractor. It is applied to a controlled loss-discovery problem with a single editable locus, where candidate artifacts are evaluated through an adaptive falsification frontier rather than static validation.
B.research_plan: The evidence uses a controlled loss-discovery problem with a single editable locus. The paper tests whether the framework rejects artifacts that static validation would have accepted and identifies the first candidate that survives the admissible falsification frontier. It then evaluates the discovered loss against CE and CE+L2 under controlled comparisons across standard benchmarks, including ImageNet, to assess transfer beyond the synthetic discovery environment.

A.problem: Autonomous AI Scientist systems are currently evaluated on reviewer scores, task completion, and experimental-information diagnostics, but not on whether the positive findings they report are actually true.
A.motivation: Scientific value ultimately rests on whether reported positive findings are true, so there is a need to make spurious discovery the headline metric and to determine where verification compute should actually be spent; oracle environments with known executable ground truth make such measurement tractable.
A.proposed_approach: An oracle-based benchmark runs full discovery loops inside environments whose executable ground truth is known, including matched control environments in which no true effect exists, so every reported positive is spurious by construction. Claim veracity is decided automatically by re-executing each reported claim's own code against freshly drawn oracle data under multiple-testing corrections. On top of this measurement layer, an independent execution-enabled adversarial refuter has the sole reward of falsifying a candidate claim before it may be reported; it is compared against a proposer-only pipeline, a self-critique pipeline, and different fractions of compute allocated to refutation.
A.research_plan: Evidence for the measurement layer is the benchmark's construction: full discovery loops, known executable ground truth, matched control environments with no true effect, and automatic re-execution with multiple-testing corrections. The central claim about adversarial refutation gating is tested by comparing the proposed refuter pipeline against the proposer-only and self-critique pipelines and across different compute fractions, while holding total compute fixed. The comparison uses oracle-measured false-discovery rate and verified discovery yield; a failure condition is that the refutation-gated pipeline does not lower false-discovery rate relative to baselines, does not retain a large share of yield, or that text-only self-critique lowers it similarly.

B.problem: End-to-end AI Scientist systems organize discovery almost entirely as greedy improvement seeking, discarding or under-reporting null and negative outcomes. Independent evaluations connect this design to overgeneralized, fragile, and occasionally fabricated claims, while existing falsification-oriented systems either run falsification outside the discovery loop or validate externally supplied hypotheses rather than steering an ongoing search.
B.motivation: Treating refutation as a scarce in-loop resource may avoid the documented fragile and overgeneralized claims, and a controller plus a benchmark with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution makes the design hypothesis testable now.
B.proposed_approach: At each step, a drop-in controller spends a budget fraction α on actively chosen refutation trials: configurations where the current claim is most likely to be contradicted. Failures gate candidate adoption, re-scope claims to the empirically supported regime, and seed the next falsification target. The paper also introduces a benchmark of regime-structured discovery tasks with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution.
B.research_plan: (1) The central hypothesis is tested by comparing a positive falsification allocation against the α = 0 greedy baseline at matched total experiment cost, with validity and calibration of claims per unit experiment budget as the evaluation target. (2) A pre-specified null finding would indicate that experiment-budget composition is not the bottleneck identified in current failure analyses and would argue against falsification-centric redesigns. The proposed benchmark of regime-structured discovery tasks with verifiable ground truth outside the search distribution provides the evaluation setting.

A.problem: Existing autonomous AI agent frameworks for scientific discovery treat hypothesis generation as an unconstrained language-model reasoning task; for bioinformatics, this leaves generated hypotheses unconstrained by biological mechanistic feasibility or experimental tractability.
A.motivation: Bioinformatics depends on hypotheses that can survive wet-lab validation, and unconstrained generation wastes effort on biologically incoherent or infeasible candidates; biological knowledge graphs and cost models now make it possible to check mechanistic coherence and feasibility during generation.
A.proposed_approach: A bioinformatics-specific agent architecture grounds hypothesis generation in biological knowledge graphs and explicitly encodes mechanistic and experimental constraints. Its core is a constraint-satisfaction layer that integrates pathway databases, gene-interaction networks, and domain-specific cost models so that candidate hypotheses are checked for mechanistic validity and experimental feasibility during generation. The agent workflow iteratively refines hypotheses by querying biological knowledge graphs and reasoning about experimental feasibility. Evaluation metrics are defined to measure hypothesis quality as novelty relative to literature and biological soundness as mechanistic validity and pathway consistency.
A.research_plan: The planned evidence is benchmark validation on two tasks: gene function hypothesis generation in systems biology, and drug repurposing with mechanistic pathway reasoning. The proposed agent will be compared against baseline LLM-only methods and hybrid approaches that apply knowledge graphs post-hoc for filtering. The key comparison targeted by the claim is whether constraint-aware generation outperforms constraint-agnostic filtering in producing hypotheses that survive wet-lab validation. No explicit ablation, matched-budget, or independent failure-condition design is stated.

B.problem: Current AI agents for scientific discovery generate hypotheses in abundance but lack principled mechanisms to prune them against the existing knowledge base before resource-intensive experimentation.
B.motivation: Principled filtering could avoid resource-intensive experiments on redundant or infeasible hypotheses while preserving novelty and discovery potential.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework augments hypothesis generation with iterative constraint-aware filtering. An LLM-based agent dynamically extracts feasibility constraints from recent photocatalysis literature and uses them to rank and eliminate redundant or infeasible hypotheses in real time. Constraint extraction is integrated into the generation loop, using a knowledge graph built from structured literature data to enforce domain-specific feasibility criteria.
B.research_plan: The evidence is a comparative evaluation on photocatalyst design spaces, benchmarking the proposed framework against hypothesis-generation-only baselines using metrics of wasted hypothesis tests, novelty, and discovery potential. No explicit failure condition or matched-resource control is stated.

A.problem: Existing LLM-based discovery agents largely rely on data-driven loss minimization alone and therefore frequently propose dimensionally inconsistent or physically implausible functional forms, wasting computational budget in combinatorial search spaces.
A.motivation: Because LLM agents now drive equation discovery, embedding dimensional constraints in their code generation and self-correction loop is feasible and can avoid wasted combinatorial search.
A.proposed_approach: A multi-agent framework that automatically extracts physical dimensions of input variables, constructs dimensionless groups, and embeds dimensional consistency checks as programmatic assertions within the agent's interactive environment, integrated into code generation, execution, and self-correction.
A.research_plan: Evaluation on symbolic regression benchmarks such as LLM-SRBench, comparing the proposed framework against unconstrained agentic baselines on invalid search trajectories and symbolic recovery accuracy.

B.problem: Most existing LLM-based systems for symbolic equation discovery attempt to guess equations directly from data, without modeling the multi-step reasoning process scientists follow—first inferring intermediate physical properties such as symmetries and then using them as priors to constrain candidate equations.
B.motivation: Symbolic, interpretable formulas are a fundamental goal of science, and LLMs' broad domain knowledge and reasoning capabilities make it valuable to encode scientist-like multi-step inference into automated equation discovery.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework is an agentic system that explicitly follows a scientist-like reasoning process. It coordinates physics-based tools to extract intermediate structure, such as physical properties and symmetries, and then uses these results to configure symbolic regression engines such as PySINDy and PySR, including their function libraries and structural constraints.
B.research_plan: The evidence is comparative benchmark evaluation: the framework is tested on a suite of physical equation benchmarks under noisy data, and its symbolic accuracy and robustness are compared with both LLM-based and traditional baselines.

A.problem: LLM-based equation-discovery agents treat data as given, proposing and refining hypotheses over a fixed dataset, so any out-of-distribution robustness is inherited from priors rather than earned from evidence. An independent 2025 evaluation also found that LLM agents used for closed-loop optimization show no sensitivity to experimental feedback.
A.motivation: Treating each measurement as an internal decision would let an agent gather evidence where rival hypotheses differ most, making robust symbolic recovery possible under fixed measurement budgets.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed agent maintains a pool of structurally rival symbolic hypotheses and, each round, asks the oracle to measure at inputs where the rivals' predictions diverge most. It combines the LLM's structural reasoning about where rival forms must differ with a numerical disagreement score that approximates expected information gain. Observed points refit and prune the pool by an information criterion, and survivors seed generation of the next rival forms.
A.research_plan: Evaluation uses oracle-queryable, recitation-resistant equation problems under fixed measurement budgets and scores symbolic recovery, posterior concentration, and out-of-distribution error in regions a passive sampler never reaches. The single claim is tested against passive, random-design, and uncertainty-sampling agents at equal budget; it fails if the disagreement-based design does not reach target symbolic recovery with fewer oracle calls and lower extrapolation error. Ablations isolate whether the discrimination objective or the LLM's region proposal carries the gain.

B.problem: Autonomous discovery agents are rewarded for hypotheses that fit data they happen to collect rather than for designing experiments that could refute their currently held wrong hypotheses. Existing closed-loop frameworks validate externally given hypotheses, maximize expected information gain about a single generative model's parameters, or fit fixed datasets with evolutionary search over equation forms, and none optimizes the experiment-selection objective that governs abandoning a wrong functional form: the severity of a proposed test.
B.motivation: Selecting experiments by their capacity to refute wrong structural assumptions would let discovery agents escape misspecified model classes and allocate oracle queries to tests that genuinely discipline their hypotheses.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed protocol has an agent generate a concrete predictive law plus a maintained ensemble of rival structural forms; choose each next oracle query to maximize computed refutation severity rather than parameter-information gain; pre-register a prediction interval before querying so outcomes cannot be rationalized post hoc; and revise the law only upon a pre-registered prediction failure, accumulating constraints from each refuted form. It also specifies a benchmark of controlled generative-model and symbolic environments.
B.research_plan: (1) For the comparative claim, the protocol is compared against EIG-based, random, LLM-intuition, and augmented SR-Scientist- and BoxingGym-style baseline experiment choices on a benchmark of controlled generative-model and symbolic environments under model-class misspecification, using quantitative metrics for out-of-distribution extrapolation and oracle-query count; support requires better extrapolation and fewer queries than those baselines. (2) For the severity-prediction claim, the study tests whether measured severity of chosen experiments predicts downstream extrapolation error across agents. Ablations isolate the severity objective, the rival ensemble, and the commit-before-query rule.

A.problem: LLM-agent AI scientist systems generate far more candidate hypotheses than compute budgets can run, but existing pipelines commit the full experiment budget at selection time, so execution failures, non-reproducibility, and late falsifications appear only after much of the budget is spent.
A.motivation: A gate that rejects non-runnable or cheaply falsified hypotheses before full experiments could reallocate scarce compute to promising candidates and reduce wasted experiment effort.
A.proposed_approach: Each candidate hypothesis must first be compiled into a pre-registered test card and then pass a cheap sandbox probe with a three-way verdict: pass, cheaply falsified, or not-runnable. The remaining experiment budget is reallocated only among hypotheses that pass, under a type-I-controlled pruning rule. The approach is evaluated using a budgeted benchmark assembled from existing research-agent and experimental-design environments, with all scores computed from workflow trace logs rather than final papers, and applied to representative AI-scientist pipelines with ablations of probe cost, falsification, reproducibility checking, and bounded repair.
A.research_plan: The three a priori claims are settled through a budgeted benchmark assembled from existing research-agent and experimental-design environments, with scores computed from workflow trace logs. (1) The yield and pruning claims are tested by evaluating the proposed gate on representative AI-scientist pipelines at matched compute and novelty against best-of-k self-confidence and AI-reviewer scoring. (2) The waste claim is measured from committed experiment compute on late-discovered failures in un-gated pipelines. (3) Probe quality is assessed via success AUC and false-pruning rate; ablations isolate probe cost, falsification, reproducibility checking, and bounded repair.

B.problem: End-to-end AI-scientist and ML-engineering agents spend most of their compute on full experiment runs, a large share of which are later invalidated, fabricated, or wrong; it is not known how to allocate a fixed total-compute budget between cheap refutation tests and full runs so that only hypotheses likely to survive are escalated.
B.motivation: Because these agents are increasingly used for high-cost experimentation, wasted compute directly limits how much reliable scientific or engineering output can be obtained; making falsification explicit and budgeted is the cheapest way to improve reliability.
B.proposed_approach: The approach formalizes falsification as a cost-aware sequential decision problem: under a fixed total-compute budget, choose which cheap refutation test to run next and when to escalate to full execution. It instantiates this as a drop-in module around existing research agents. Before any candidate hypothesis may spend expensive compute, the agent must derive, pre-register, and execute the cheapest executable test that could refute it; only hypotheses that survive or are cheaply killed under a calibrated decision rule are escalated. The work also introduces two evaluation targets: the fraction of completed, empirically confirmed artifacts per unit compute, and the fraction of expensive compute wasted on hypotheses later refuted.
B.research_plan: Evidence comes from comparing the proposed module against end-to-end and proxy-scoring baselines under equal total compute, using the confirmed-artifact-rate and wasted-expensive-compute metrics plus hypothesis novelty and ideation diversity. Support requires higher confirmed-artifact rate and lower wasted expensive compute than both baselines while novelty and ideation diversity do not fall; failure is the absence of improvement on either compute-efficiency metric or any reduction in novelty or ideation diversity.

A.problem: Quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale.
A.motivation: Making quantitative evidence synthesis scalable would support reliable, evidence-based decision-making across science, medicine, education, and policy.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed system is an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, it formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, performs random-effects meta-analysis, supports heterogeneity analysis across moderators and risk-of-bias assessment, and outputs a transparent PRISMA-aligned report.
A.research_plan: (1) The end-to-end capability claim is exercised by applying the system to a research question and having it produce a PRISMA-aligned report after screening candidate studies and extracting quantitative claims. (2) The agreement claim is tested by comparing the system's pooled effect estimates with expert-conducted meta-analyses using Hedges' g; close agreement is support, and lack of close agreement would count against the claim.

B.problem: Recent LLM-based systems automate article screening, data extraction, and qualitative synthesis in systematic reviews, but the quantitative meta-analysis phase — pooling extracted data, managing heterogeneity, and drawing consensus — remains largely manual.
B.motivation: Automating this phase would remove a labor-intensive bottleneck in evidence-based science and scale systematic review synthesis.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed LLM-agent framework combines structured data extraction with intelligent conflict detection, feeds heterogeneous evidence into statistical meta-analysis engines, and uses reasoning agents to interpret results, flag publication bias and methodological concerns, and generate interpretable synthesis narratives. A pilot implementation targets biomedical meta-analyses.
B.research_plan: A pilot implementation targeting biomedical meta-analyses will be used to demonstrate automation of study-level pooling, heterogeneity analysis, sensitivity testing, and generation of human-auditable evidence summaries; these demonstrations serve as the evidence for the framework's end-to-end automation and scalability claims. No named baselines, comparative metrics, or explicit failure conditions are stated.

A.problem: Generating high-quality hypotheses in scientific research is challenging and time-consuming, and current LLM-based approaches show promise but can be further improved in effectiveness.
A.motivation: Automating hypothesis generation could reduce the time and effort required for scientific research; recent advances in LLMs make this tractable, and evolutionary algorithms are well-suited for exploring complex search spaces and optimizing solutions.
A.proposed_approach: The proposed work develops a framework that integrates LLMs with evolutionary algorithms to automate and optimize hypothesis generation. The evolutionary algorithm component is used to explore complex search spaces and optimize candidate solutions, while LLMs support hypothesis generation.
A.research_plan: The framework will be evaluated across various scientific domains to assess performance, efficiency, and innovation. No baselines, metrics, or failure conditions are specified, and no matched controls or ablations are described.

B.problem: Existing LLM-assisted approaches to scientific idea generation exhibit semantic convergence, which limits the diversity and novelty of generated research ideas.
B.motivation: As LLMs show promise in assisting idea generation, overcoming semantic convergence is valuable for broadening the candidate ideas and advancing scientific progress.
B.proposed_approach: The proposed framework recasts scientific idea generation as an evolutionary search over a population of ideas. It iteratively applies rank-based mutation with differentiated retrieval planning to incorporate external knowledge, and semantic-aware crossover to fuse complementary concepts for conceptual reorganization. A lightweight evaluation signal guides selection, encouraging sustained exploration while mitigating premature convergence.
B.research_plan: The evidence is extensive experiments comparing the proposed framework to state-of-the-art baselines on novelty, diversity, and idea quality under the current automatic evaluation protocol. Claims about enhanced exploration and maintained quality are supported by these comparisons; no explicit failure condition is stated in the abstract.

A.problem: Rigorous real-world physical research using large language models is stalled by a lack of realistic evaluation benchmarks and by systemic LLM hallucinations.
A.motivation: Addressing these barriers would make automated scientific discovery in quantum many-body simulation more robust, reliable, and transparent.
A.proposed_approach: The work releases a research-level benchmark of 100 tasks in quantum many-body simulation drawn from 21 high-impact journals. The proposed framework is a multi-agent system that enforces self-verification and error correction; it integrates programming verifiers and scientific verifiers to check coding correctness and principle-based physical validity, producing interpretable evidence and error correction at each step.
A.research_plan: (1) The claim that the benchmark is research-level and challenging rests on its construction from 100 tasks in 21 high-impact journals and on testing against current frontier LLMs. (2) The claim that the framework enforces reliable, physically valid outputs rests on comparisons with existing LLM baselines across benchmark scenarios and on evaluation of inference-time scaling.

B.problem: Current language agents in autonomous AI scientist systems frequently fail during complex, multi-step experimental execution and validation because they lack adequate error correction and rigorous intermediate verification; this produces an implementation gap between generated research plans and executable, validated results.
B.motivation: As autonomous scientist systems become more capable at generating hypotheses, code, and reports, trustworthy adoption depends on closing the implementation gap so that agent-produced work is executable and its conclusions reliable.
B.proposed_approach: The framework integrates constraint-guided test-time verification and dynamic self-correction loops into autonomous scientific workflows. Scientific verification is decomposed into domain-specific invariant checking, automated test case synthesis, and executable code validation. Test-time interaction and verification compute are scaled to catch errors before conclusions are finalized.
B.research_plan: The comparative claim is evaluated on challenging scientific agent benchmarks against standard prompting and unverified iterative debugging baselines, measuring execution success rates and reliability of discovered findings. The detection claim is addressed through the framework's decomposition into invariant checking, test synthesis, and code validation, though no explicit failure condition or ablation is stated.

A.problem: Current autonomous AI research agents can detect and localize individual task failures through trajectory analysis and error attribution, but they do not learn to adapt their core research strategy—hypothesis generation, experiment prioritization, or resource allocation—based on systematic patterns of failures across multiple trials within a domain.
A.motivation: Agents that adapt their research strategy from failure patterns could achieve higher discovery rates, lower per-task cost, and faster convergence to effective research methods, making autonomous discovery more efficient.
